title: 2-D grid DP
summary: When moves only go right or down, the answer for a cell depends only on the cell above and the cell to its left. Fill the grid row by row and every input is ready when you need it.
idea: dp[r][c] = combine(dp[r − 1][c], dp[r][c − 1]) plus this cell. Handle the first row, the first column and blocked cells, then fill top-left to bottom-right.

signals.see: A grid, and you may move only right and down (or in another fixed pair of directions).
signals.think: No cycles are possible, so the grid itself is the DP table and row-major order is a valid fill order.

signals.see: Count the paths, or find the cheapest path, from one corner to the opposite corner.
signals.think: Counting sums the neighbours; cheapest takes the min of the neighbours and adds the cell's own cost.

signals.see: 'Largest square of 1s' or similar shape questions.
signals.think: Store the best shape whose bottom-right corner is this cell. It is built from the up, left and up-left cells.

phrasings: How many routes does a robot have from the top-left to the bottom-right, avoiding blocked cells?
Find the cheapest way across a grid of tolls, moving only right or down.
Find the largest square of free cells on a floor plan.

picture.title: Walking every route versus filling cells in order
picture.alt: On the left, every route is walked from the start, and routes share long stretches that are walked again and again. On the right, each cell is filled once, row by row, from the cell above and the cell to its left.
picture.caption: Each cell reads only its up and left neighbours.

visualiser.inputHelp: Rows of 0 (open) and 1 (blocked), separated by /. Up to 5 rows and 5 columns. Moves go right or down.

oneLiner: for r, for c: dp[r][c] = cell + combine(dp[r-1][c], dp[r][c-1]); edges have one neighbour

exercise.prompt: Each cell of the grid holds a toll of 0 or more. Start at the top-left, move only right or down, and return the least total toll to reach the bottom-right, counting both end cells. The starter treats the missing neighbour outside the grid as a free 0.
hints: dp[r][c] is the least toll to reach cell (r, c). The start cell costs just its own toll.
You arrive from above or from the left, so dp[r][c] = grid[r][c] + min(up, left).
A neighbour outside the grid does not exist: use infinity so min ignores it, not 0.

complexity.space: O(R × C), or O(C) with one row
complexity.why: Every cell is filled once with constant work. Each row reads only the row above, so a single row array can be reused.

mistakes: Treating cells outside the grid as 0 when minimising, which makes the edges look free.
Forgetting blocked cells, or not setting the start to 0 ways when it is blocked.
Filling column by column in an order where the left neighbour is not ready.
Mixing up rows and columns in grid[r][c] for non-square grids.

quiz.question: Why does row-by-row, left-to-right order work for right/down moves?
choices: The cell above and the cell to the left are always filled first
quiz.explain: A valid fill order puts every input before the cell that reads it.

quiz.question: When counting paths, what goes in a blocked cell?
quiz.explain: A 0 also stops paths flowing through it to later cells.

quiz.question: For the largest square of 1s, a cell's side is…
choices: 1 + min(up, left, up-left) for a 1 cell
quiz.explain: The smallest of the three neighbours limits how far the square can grow.

interviewTip: Mention the row-array space saving after the full table works. Interviewers like to hear it, but get the 2-D version right first.
